einzeiler: Exploring the centuries-old economic roots of private space exploration and public policy.
kurzfassung: This episode explores the economic history of space exploration, arguing that private investment and billionaire-funded projects predate NASA by over a century. Host Casey Dreyer and guest Alex MacDonald examine how historical astronomical observatories parallel modern commercial spaceflight. They also discuss the concepts of signaling and prestige in shaping public and private space policy.
stichpunkte: Private funding for space exploration began long before NASA, notably with wealthy 19th-century observatory patrons.
The classic narrative of government-led space exploration starting only after Sputnik is incomplete.
Space activities serve as costly signals of national capability and cooperation rather than mere prestige.
Historical civic observatories relied on grassroots crowd-funding models similar to modern platforms.
Wealth inequality throughout history has consistently enabled wealthy individuals to fund massive astronomical projects.
Robert Goddard utilized a mix of private philanthropic grants from the Guggenheim family and military funding.
Negative signaling explains why governments continue funding human spaceflight once capabilities are established.
The modern rise of billionaire-funded space efforts mirrors the Gilded Age pattern of monumental scientific patronage.

beschreibung:
We tend to think of private space exploration as a recent phenomenon. But as Alex MacDonald, former Chief Economist at NASA, argues in his book "The Long Space Age," privately funded space exploration has deep roots in American history, stretching back more than two centuries.
In this 2017 conversation with The Planetary Society's Chief of Space Policy Casey Dreier, originally aired on the Space Policy Edition of Planetary Radio, MacDonald traces the economic history of American space exploration from the 1769 transit of Venus all the way to the present day, and makes the case that the government-dominated model we grew up with may actually be the historical anomaly.
